shortDescription: Reliance Communications’ (RCom) Committee of Creditors (CoC) has asked the Enforcement Directorate (ED) and the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (IBBI) to release the company’s real estate properties worth ₹7,000 crore, following the Supreme Court’s rejection of the spectrum insolvency plea…

children: Reliance Communications’ (RCom) Committee of Creditors (CoC) has asked the Enforcement Directorate (ED) and the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (IBBI) to release the company’s real estate properties worth ₹7,000 crore, following the Supreme Court’s rejection of the spectrum insolvency plea. The creditors are likely to meet this week to deliberate on further resolution possibilities, according to the information accessed by businessline.

Shortly after the Supreme Court refused to reconsider spectrum as an asset under the insolvency code, the Committee, led by State Bank of India, is seeking to preserve and unlock the value of the company’s remaining assets—particularly its real estate portfolio. This includes 132.07 acres of land at Dhirubhai Ambani Knowledge City (DAKC) in Navi Mumbai, valued at ₹4,462.81 crore, which was attached by the ED in the last year. Accounting for other attached real estate properties in Delhi, Chennai, Pune and Odisha, the total value of attached assets is estimated to exceed ₹7,000 crore.

Real estate has assumed an important role in RCom’s resolution, particularly after the exclusion of spectrum from the insolvency pool. The original resolution plan estimated recoveries of over ₹23,000 crore for 38 lenders against secured debt of approximately ₹33,000 crore. For the highest bidder of the company’s core assets, UV Asset Reconstruction Company Ltd. (UVARCL), spectrum accounted for more than half of the proposed consideration of approximately ₹14,000 crore.

With that asset no longer available, the property portfolio is to be one of the principal sources of value for creditors to support a new resolution plan or generate recoveries through liquidation. However, a significant portion of the real estate has been provisionally attached by the ED, restricting sale, transfer or otherwise monetisation of the properties. Other assets include the enterprise business, data centre assets and recoveries from legal claims. The CoC’s request to the ED to release the attached properties is thus central to the future of RCOM’s resolution process.

The committee is expected to meet this Friday to evaluate the available options in light of the Supreme Court’s spectrum judgment and the subsequent dismissal of the review petition. The first alternative for the CoC is to restart the resolution process with revised asset valuations, reflecting current market realities and ED attachment benchmarks. Failing this, the next alternative is liquidation. RCom’s real estate holdings may be significant for creditor recoveries, but actual recoveries would depend on the ability to realise the assets.

title: Reliance Communications’ Creditors request ED to release real estate properties worth ₹7,000 crore
